data.title: Dangling DNS Records Permit Subdomain Takeover
data.summary: DNS records pointed at cloud resources that had been released, so the name could be claimed by registering the same resource. Content then served from a hostname the organisation owns, with its certificate and its reputation behind it.
data.description:
A subdomain takeover is a decommissioning failure. A service is created, a CNAME is pointed at it, the service is later deleted — and the CNAME stays. Anyone who registers that resource name receives traffic for the organisation's hostname.

What follows is worse than defacement. The attacker holds a hostname under the corporate domain, can obtain a valid certificate for it, and can set cookies scoped to the parent domain where those are in use. Phishing hosted there survives every check a user is taught to make, because the domain genuinely is the company's.

The records involved are usually old marketing sites, event microsites, status pages and documentation hosts — exactly the assets nobody owns after the project ends.
data.recommendation:
* Make DNS cleanup part of decommissioning, and verify it rather than assuming it.
* Scan your zones for records resolving to unclaimed resources, continuously rather than annually.
* Keep an owner against every record, so a name with no owner is itself a finding.
* Prefer records pointing at infrastructure you control over third-party hostnames where the choice exists.
data.short_recommendation: Remove DNS records when the resource behind them is released.
